title: Common Elements, Min Count
statement:
You get two integer arrays, A and B. Some numbers appear in both, possibly several times.

For every value v that appears in both arrays, take min(count of v in A, count of v in B). Add those minimums up.

Write def solution(A, B) that returns that sum as an int. Put another way: it is the size of the multiset intersection, the number of elements you can pair off one from A with an equal one from B, each element used at most once.

examples.why: 2 is in A twice and in B three times: min is 2. 3 is in each once: 1. 1 and 4 are in only one array. 2 + 1 = 3.
Only one 5 in B can be paired, so the min is 1, not 3.
No value is in both arrays.

constraints: arrays are not sorted; hidden tests are large enough that O(N × M) times out

think.q: The OA wording was reported as "framed very weirdly". Restate it in your own words before you code.
think.a: The report paraphrased it as: numbers in 2 arrays repeated in both, take the min of the occurrence counts and add it to the result. That means: count each value in A, count each value in B, and for shared values add the smaller count. The report does not say whether you add the count or the value times the count, so check your reading against the sample output before you write code. Say it back as "the size of the multiset intersection".
Counts in A: {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 1}. Counts in B: {2: 3, 3: 1, 4: 1}. Shared values 2 and 3: min(2, 3) + min(1, 1) = 3.

think.q: What is the first correct thing you could write?
think.a: Copy B into a list. For each a in A, if a is in the list, remove one copy and add 1. Correct, but in and remove are O(M) each, so O(N × M): 10^10 steps at the limits.
"occurrence count" and "in both" → hashing with counters. A dict (or collections.Counter) turns "how many times does v appear" into an O(1) lookup.

1. Build count_a = Counter(A) and count_b = Counter(B).
  2. Loop over the values of the smaller counter.
  3. If the value is in the other counter, add the smaller of the two counts.
  4. Return the total.

One or both arrays empty (0). No overlap (0). One value repeated many times on one side only. Negative numbers and zero (dict keys handle them, but a fixed-size count array would not). Identical arrays (answer is the full length).

hints: Restate the task as "how many pairs (one from A, one from B) of equal values can I make, using each element once?" Then check it gives 3 on the first example.
For one value v, the number of pairs is min(countA[v], countB[v]). So you only need the counts, not the positions.

Use collections.Counter. sum((Counter(A) & Counter(B)).values()) is a one-liner and passes. In a live round, be ready to say what & does on two Counters: it keeps each shared key with the smaller count.
explain:
The hard part of this OA question is reading it, not coding it. Before writing anything, restate it and test the restatement on the example:

  • "For each value in both arrays, the smaller of its two counts, summed."
  • On A = [1, 2, 2, 3], B = [2, 2, 2, 3, 4]: value 2 gives min(2, 3) = 2, value 3 gives min(1, 1) = 1. Total 3, which matches.

If your restatement does not match the sample output, your reading is wrong. That check takes one minute and saves the whole question. In a proctored HackerRank OA you cannot ask anyone, so the samples are your only clarification.

The code is two counters and one loop. Looping over the smaller counter keeps the work at O(N + M) to build and O(min distinct) to compare.
complexity: O(N + M) time, O(distinct values) extra space

tests.label: B is empty
tests.why: A has more distinct values than B, so the solution swaps the counters: the swap must not crash

tests.label: A has more distinct values
tests.why: 5 gives min(2, 1) = 1, 6 gives 1; the loop runs over B's counter after the swap

tests.label: zeros
tests.why: zero is a normal value: min(2, 3) = 2

tests.label: identical arrays
tests.why: every element pairs: answer is the full length

tests.label: skewed counts
tests.why: each side has many copies of the value the other side has few of

tests.label: extreme values
tests.why: values at the limits are just dict keys

tests.label: mixed 30 x 26
tests.why: many shared values with different counts

govtech.evidence: A 2026 GovTech OA report (Glassdoor snippet, unverified) describes adding up min(count in A, count in B) for numbers that appear in both arrays, a variant of LeetCode 350, and says the question was "framed very weirdly". It is unclear whether the counts or the values were summed; this page sums the counts.
extensions: Return the sum of v * min(countA[v], countB[v]) instead of the count: the same loop, one changed line.
Return the intersection itself as a sorted list with repeats, e.g. [2, 2, 3].
Both arrays are already sorted. Do it in O(1) extra space with two pointers: advance the pointer at the smaller value, and on a match count it and advance both.
B is too large for memory and arrives as a stream. Keep only Counter(A) and decrement it as matches arrive.
